clues: Located in the rostral ventrolateral medulla, it contains intrinsic pacemaker neurons
Opioids bind mu-receptors here to depress breathing frequency
It functions as the primary rhythm generator for automatic inspiration
Located in the upper pons (parabrachial / Kolliker-Fuse nucleus), it inhibits the apneustic center
Strong stimulation shortens inspiratory duration, reduces tidal volume, and increases respiratory rate
It regulates the switch-off point of the medullary inspiratory ramp signal
Located in the lower pons, it sends tonic excitatory drive to medullary inspiratory neurons
Interruption of both the upper pontine center and the vagus nerves leaves it uninhibited
Unopposed activity produces prolonged inspiratory spasms interrupted by brief expiratory gasps
Located near the ventral surface of the medulla, they sense hydrogen ions in cerebrospinal fluid
Because CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier freely while H+ does not, they respond rapidly to arterial hypercapnia
They account for roughly 70 to 80 percent of the steady-state ventilatory response to CO2
Situated at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries, they signal via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Hypoxia closes O2-sensitive K+ channels in their Type I glomus cells, triggering depolarization and Ca2+ influx
They are the sole chemoreceptors in humans mediating the ventilatory response to arterial hypoxemia

terms.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
clues: Slowly adapting smooth muscle stretch receptors send signals via myelinated vagal afferents
In adults it activates at tidal volumes above ~1 to 1.5 liters to prevent lung overdistension
It inhibits medullary inspiratory neurons upon marked pulmonary expansion

terms.sub: Pulmonary and Airway Reflexes (Hering-Breuer, J-Receptors, Irritant)
clues: Located in alveolar walls adjacent to pulmonary capillaries, they signal via unmyelinated vagal C-fibers
Pulmonary capillary congestion, interstitial edema, and pulmonary embolism stimulate them
Their activation produces rapid, shallow breathing (tachypnea) and the sensation of dyspnea
It is classically seen in severe metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis
Peripheral carotid body chemoreceptors initiate it in response to falling arterial pH
It manifests as deep, rapid, labored hyperventilation aimed at blowing off CO2
In severe congestive heart failure, prolonged lung-to-brain circulation delay precipitates this pattern
It also occurs during sleep at high altitude and after bilateral cerebral hemispheric injury
It consists of smooth crescendo-decrescendo cycles of tidal volume separated by regular central apneas
Congenital cases are commonly linked to mutations in the PHOX2B transcription factor gene
Voluntary corticospinal breathing remains intact during wakefulness, while automatic metabolic drive fails
Patients develop severe hypoventilation and life-threatening central apnea as soon as they fall asleep
